title: How does `this` work in JavaScript?
description: The four binding rules — default, implicit, explicit, and new — plus arrow functions and why this behaves differently from other languages.

data.text: `this` is determined **at call time, not definition time**, by four rules applied in order: (1) **explicit** — `call`/`apply`/`bind` set it directly; (2) **new** — a constructor call creates a fresh object and binds `this` to it; (3) **implicit** — `obj.method()` binds `this` to `obj`; (4) **default** — otherwise, in sloppy mode `this` is the global object (undefined in strict mode/modules). Arrow functions have **no own `this`** — they capture `this` lexically from the surrounding function, which is why they're ideal for callbacks that must see the enclosing context. That call-time binding is why React class methods detach (`onClick={this.handleClick}` loses `this`) and why `bind` exists.

**The four rules in detail:**
- **Explicit**: `fn.call(thisArg, a, b)`, `fn.apply(thisArg, [a, b])`, `const bound = fn.bind(thisArg)` — bind returns a permanently new function with `this` fixed forever; call/apply invoke immediately
- **new**: `new Foo()` → creates object, its `[[Prototype]]` is Foo.prototype, `this` inside Foo is that object, and unless the constructor returns an object, that object is the result
- **Implicit**: `person.greet()` → `this === person`; the object left of the dot is the receiver — and destructuring or reassigning loses it: `const greet = person.greet; greet()` → this is no longer person
- **Default**: bare `fn()` → globalThis in sloppy mode, `undefined` in strict mode (all ES modules are strict)

**Arrow functions:**
- Lexical this: captured from the enclosing function scope at definition — they cannot be bound (`bind`/`call` on arrows has no effect), can't be constructors
- Perfect for callbacks inside methods: `setTimeout(() => this.tick(), 100)` keeps the method's this; `setTimeout(this.tick.bind(this))` is the equivalent non-arrow fix

**Common real-world manifestations:**
- React class components: `this.setState` in callbacks — hence constructor binding, class fields with arrows (`handleClick = () => {}`), or just use function components with hooks
- Detached method references in general: `const log = console.log; log('x')` — usually fine for console, disastrous for methods that use this
- Passing `obj.method` to forEach/map: `items.forEach(obj.process)` — obj is lost; wrap: `(x) => obj.process(x)`
- Strict mode/module surprises: `this` is undefined, so `this.x = 1` at top level throws

**Precedence note:** explicit bind beats implicit object; there's no rule conflict once you check in that order. ES2023's `Function.prototype.prototype` and explicit-resource methods aside, the four rules cover everything.

data.title: Each rule, and the classic losses of `this`

data.text:
Interviewers want to assess:
- The four-rule model and that binding happens at call time
- Arrow functions have lexical this and ignore bind/call
- Real failure modes: detached methods, callbacks in class components
- Knowing when explicit binding (bind in constructor, class fields) is needed vs when it isn't

items: Assuming this works like Java/C# static scoping — it's call-site dependent
Passing a method as a bare callback and losing the receiver
Using regular functions in setTimeout inside methods, then wondering why this is undefined
Calling bind on an arrow function and expecting it to rebind
Forgetting modules are strict — top-level this is undefined, not globalThis
Re-binding on every render in React (bind in JSX) — use class fields or arrows instead
How does super() affect this in derived constructors?
What does 'this' mean in an object literal method vs a standalone function?
Why do class fields with arrow functions avoid the binding problem?
How does bind compare with the latest-ref pattern in React hooks?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: this is set at call time: explicit (call/apply/bind) > new > implicit (dot) > default
Arrow functions inherit this lexically and cannot be rebound
Detached methods lose their receiver — the classic callback bug
Modules run in strict mode: bare calls give this === undefined
data.takeaway: Ask 'what's left of the dot at the call site?' — that one question answers where this points in every JavaScript scenario.
